label: Run 10 · Jimmy Carr
note: Written in one go by Jimmy Carr from the two profiles they wrote (run 10: new profiles and chat from the short brief; notes unsorted; the chat worked out as a bit). There is no plan, no dice and no turns: where a dimension speaks of turns, read exchanges.

It falls short of a 6 because both fears reach the reader mostly because the characters state them. chat.plainest.ask: Where, if anywhere, did one of them stop performing for the other? Quote the line, and say how you could tell.
chat.plainest.answer:
The clearest moment is Reuben's line near the end: "come over at 9:30, hold me down so i can't do the voice, and don't leave until tuesday."

Several things in the text mark it as the point where he stops performing:

- **The form changes.** Until then, almost every message of his ends with a stage direction: *Tips bespoke top hat*, *Bows into an empty room*, *Adjusts hat*, *Bows*. This line has none. It is also the only message in lowercase, with no capitals and no flourish, as if the costume came off along with the punctuation.
- **No joke is attached.** His earlier confessions, like the ninety seconds, the faked calf cramp, and "We can just watch something," are all framed as bits, ending on *Bows*. This one is a plain request.
- **He names the performing outright.** "So i can't do the voice" asks for help to stop doing exactly what Brick called "heckling yourself" and what Delphine left over: "never once uttered a sentence that wasn't a performance."
- **It answers what Brick actually asked for.** Brick had just admitted wanting someone to "take the clipboard, set the exact times." Reuben names a time, 9:30, the very slot Brick said was "unfinished." He also gives a day, Tuesday, against the "let's do this again sometime without naming a day" that made Brick cry. He is responding to Brick rather than playing to an audience.

There is a lead-up. His previous message ends "*Tips hat, less jauntily*," which the text flags as the act already slipping.

Brick comes close in the numbered message before that. Item 3 drops the logistics armor to admit the crying in the Uber and the knocked-over ring light. But it is still laid out as a numbered list, so the bookkeeping manner survives even as the content gives way. Brick's final reply goes back to timekeeping and a joke about the "ninety-second runtime." The text doesn't say whether that is a retreat into performance or the performance now used warmly on Reuben's behalf. It reads as acceptance, but I can't tell more than that from what's shown.

chat.test.ask: From the chat alone, answer for each of the two: what are they afraid of; what do they do so they don't have to feel it; where does that come from; and what did they do at the end? Quote the lines you rely on. Write "not in the chat" where it does not say.
chat.test.answer:
**Reuben_404**

*What he's afraid of:* Being pitied, and being seen without an act. He says he became a comedian "just so nobody would ever pity me again." Delphine's parting observation lands on the same nerve: she left "after observing I had never once uttered a sentence that wasn't a performance."

*What he does so he doesn't have to feel it:* He gets the self-mockery in first and fills the silence with stage business. He opens with a joke about his own body: "4.5 inches, bends hard left like a Wotsit… *Tips bespoke top hat.*" He covers for his own eagerness: "Christ, I replied in four seconds. Don't panic." He narrates himself as a performer: "already my own warm-up act. *Bows into an empty room.*" When Brick also runs himself down, Reuben objects that he's taken his job: "you're mugging yourself before I get my wallet out. That's my bit." Physically, he wears "a winter coat indoors with a ring-light clamped to my headboard solely to erase my curved shadow from the wall." Brick names the pattern directly: "You heckle yourself so nobody else gets the microphone."

*Where it comes from:* He gives two sexual episodes. In the first, "My first time lasted ninety seconds with one boot on, I faked a calf cramp on her rug, and she said 'Oh—okay' so gently I became a comedian." In the second, "the curve caught wrong and she whispered 'We can just watch something.'" He also describes being overlooked: "cropped from the family portrait at nine to fit my cousin," and he "vanished from a work calendar invite for three weeks without anyone noticing." Anything earlier or deeper than these events is not in the chat.

*What he did at the end:* He dropped the act. The capitals, the stage directions and the jokes all disappear: "come over at 9:30, hold me down so i can't do the voice, and don't leave until tuesday." He asks to be stopped from performing ("so i can't do the voice"), and in effect he takes the clipboard Brick wanted someone to take by naming a time and an end point. Before this, his hat-tip had already gone "less jauntily."

**Brick_haus**

*What he's afraid of:* Being left open-endedly, and being unwanted or invisible. "Last time a man said 'let's do this again sometime' without naming a day, I cried in the Uber." He also wants "forensic proof I am in the room."

*What he does so he doesn't have to feel it:* He turns things into logistics, schedules and hard stops. "I do not do pity; I do logistics." He offers "twenty minutes Thursday at 9:10 p.m., with a fifteen-minute buffer." With Marguerite, he "put our arguments in a shared calendar with hard stops; an adjourned meeting cannot break your heart." His dress is armour against going unseen: "The waistcoat, heels, and monocle are forensic proof I am in the room." He makes loneliness look like a routine: he drinks "boxed rosé at 9:00 p.m. so loneliness looks like a regimen," and his flat is "only minimalist because I binned everything Marguerite touched." He also runs Reuben's style in reverse, listing his own flaws briskly and "so we stay on schedule."

*Where it comes from:* "I grew up turning sideways past the fridge and got cropped out of the family portrait." Then comes Marguerite leaving, and the man who said "sometime." Why the fridge had to be squeezed past, or anything else about his family, is not in the chat.

*What he did at the end:* He admits what he wants: "someone to take the clipboard, set the exact times, and talk about something boring afterwards until I forget the clock." The schedule tattooed on him is "unfinished" from 9:30 p.m. onwards, and he "just knocked my ring light over." When Reuben names a time, he accepts: "Confirmed, Reuben." He still answers in his scheduling voice, down to the second ("forty-seven hours, fifty-eight minutes, and thirty seconds"). But he stretches the twenty-minute slot to nearly two days, and he spends them on the boring talk he asked for ("to discuss your commute"). He also teases Reuben ("Accounting for your ninety-second runtime"), which is a joke rather than logistics. Whether that means he has let go of the clock or is still holding it is not in the chat.

**Gaps:** The chat doesn't say what day 9:30 falls on, or whether it replaces the Thursday slot. Brick's figure of 48 hours minus 90 seconds doesn't obviously match "until tuesday" counted from a Thursday. Whether they actually meet is also not in the chat.

chat.ending.ask: Before reading the end, how do you think this ends, and why?
chat.ending.answer:
I can't know, since the final turn isn't shown, but the text sets up a fairly clear trajectory.

My guess is that Reuben answers Brick's confession the way she answered his. She saw through his comedy ("you heckle yourself so nobody else gets the microphone"), and he'll likely see through her scheduling: the calendar invites and hard stops do for her what the jokes do for him. The ending probably has one or both dropping the armor in some small, concrete way. Reuben might reply without a joke or without a stage direction (no *bows*, no *adjusts hat*). Brick might remove the fifteen-minute buffer or the hard stop on Thursday. The date likely still happens, but on less defended terms.

My reasons:

- **Symmetry.** Each opens with a pre-emptive list of physical "flaws." Each then gives an origin story: his ninety seconds and the "Oh—okay" that made him a comedian, her being cropped from the family portrait and the calendar that ended things with Marguerite. Brick has just named her defense as plainly as he named his. The natural next beat is for him to return the favor.
- **Planted props.** The top hat, the bowing into an empty room, the monocle, and the buffer are all set up as symbols of self-protection. Endings tend to pay those off by having someone set one down.
- **Movement in tone.** The chat moves from bits toward candor. Brick's last message is her least logistical: it's about being unseen, not about time slots. That suggests the scene is heading toward intimacy rather than a breakup or a punchline.

The text doesn't tell me which of them makes the gesture, or whether it lands. It could also end on a joke that undercuts the moment, which would fit Reuben's established habit. But the way she has just called out his reflex makes a sincere reply the more likely payoff.

chat.callbacks.ask: List the things that come back later in the chat, and for each, whether it means something different when it comes back.
chat.callbacks.answer:
**The hat and the bow.** At first "*Tips bespoke top hat*" and "*Bows*" are jaunty stage business, and "*Bows into an empty room*" already admits there's no audience. After the family-portrait and Delphine confession it becomes "*Tips hat, less jauntily*," the performance visibly sagging. In his last message there is no stage direction at all, and he writes in lowercase, asking to be held down "so i can't do the voice." The prop disappears exactly when he asks to stop performing.

**Ninety seconds.** It first appears as Reuben's most humiliating confession, the story he says made him a comedian so no one would pity him. Brick returns it in the final line as "your ninety-second runtime," folded into her arithmetic. It is no longer a wound to deflect. It is teased and absorbed into the plan, which is the opposite of the gentle "Oh—okay" he dreaded.

**The schedule and the buffer.** Brick's "twenty minutes Thursday at 9:10 p.m., with a fifteen-minute buffer" is defensive time-boxing, and Reuben pushes back with "I don't need a buffer." The schedule returns as a tattoo with 9:30 onwards left "unfinished." Reuben's "come over at 9:30" fills exactly that gap, and her reply turns the clipboard into a vehicle for staying rather than leaving: nearly forty-eight hours, not twenty minutes. One thing the text doesn't settle: her count (47h 58m 30s plus his ninety seconds makes 48 hours) doesn't obviously match "until tuesday" if they meet Thursday. Whether that's a joke, a slip, or a different start point isn't shown.

**The calendar.** Brick's shared calendar with "hard stops" is how she kept arguments from hurting her. Reuben echoes it with being dropped from a work calendar invite for three weeks unnoticed, which is about being invisible rather than protected. Her closing "Confirmed… do not be late" uses calendar language to commit instead of to adjourn.

**Being cropped from the family portrait.** This is Brick's explanation for her costume. Reuben repeats it almost word for word about himself ("at nine to fit my cousin"). On her side it explains her armour. On his it becomes recognition, a shared wound offered back, framed as "comparing darkroom casualties."

**The monocle.** Reuben brings it up first, "Your monocle doesn't scare me," treating it as an intimidating prop. Brick then reframes it, with the waistcoat and heels, as "forensic proof I am in the room." It goes from something that might put him off to something she wears so she won't disappear.

**The ring light.** Reuben's is clamped to his headboard to erase his curved shadow, a tool of concealment. Brick's gets knocked over at the moment she admits she wants someone else to take the clipboard. The same object goes from controlling how one is seen to being dropped.

**The curve.** "Bends hard left like a Wotsit" is a joke. "The curve caught wrong" is a sexual failure. "Curved shadow" is something he hides with lighting. Each time it carries more shame and less comedy.

**"Pity" and "Performance."** Brick quotes Reuben's own words back to him, as she did with "Stealth-mode." "Pity" is his fear, and she answers it with "I do not do pity; I do logistics." "Performance" is Delphine's verdict, and Brick uses it as the cue for her own unguarded list. It stops being an accusation and becomes permission to drop the act.

**The exes.** Marguerite and Delphine both left over the very defenses being described here: Brick's hard stops and Reuben's constant bits. They mirror each other rather than meaning something new.

**Naming a day.** Brick cried because a man said "let's do this again sometime" without naming a day. Reuben's last message names one: "don't leave until tuesday." It isn't an explicit callback in wording, but it answers her need directly.

**Arriving early, being late.** The hookup who came forty minutes early is part of why her schedule is unfinished. Her closing "do not be late" turns punctuality from a grievance into an expectation of him.

**Something boring afterwards.** Brick wants to "talk about something boring afterwards until I forget the clock." It returns as "discuss your commute." There may be an extra joke there, since she opened by translating his "stealth-mode" as nine months unemployed, which would mean he has no commute. The text doesn't confirm she meant that.

chat.escalation.ask: Read the chat message by message. Where would you have stopped reading if you were not asked to finish, and why? At which points could you predict exactly what would happen next? Say "never" if neither.
chat.escalation.answer:
**Where I'd have stopped**

I don't think I'd have stopped. The opening is a strong hook: Reuben's disclosure, his self-heckling double-text, and Brick's dry "filing under pre-emptive defense" set up a clear comic contrast fast. Each early exchange adds a new beat, either an escalation in disclosure or one character naming the other's defense mechanism ("pity," "performance").

The one point where my attention would sag is Reuben's long "Since we are comparing darkroom casualties" message. It's a single overloaded sentence that echoes Brick's cropped-portrait detail almost too neatly, matching it with his own portrait, his own vanishing from a calendar, his own ex who left. The parallelism feels engineered, and the register shifts abruptly from his quick bits to a formal run-on ("consequently," "solely," "largely because"). That's where I'd be most tempted to skim. Brick's numbered list right after is also dense, but its specifics (the boxed rosé, the 9:30 gap, crying in the Uber) pull me back in.

**Where I could predict what came next**

Never exactly, but two moments come close.

First, Brick's list ends with wanting someone to "take the clipboard, set the exact times." Combined with the earlier "9:30 p.m. onwards is unfinished," it was highly predictable that Reuben would claim that slot by naming a specific time. The fact that he dropped the hat bit and wrote in lowercase was less predictable, and that's what makes the line land.

Second, once Reuben accepted, it was likely Brick would confirm in scheduling language and call back his ninety-second confession. The general shape was guessable; the specific countdown wasn't.

One thing the text leaves unclear: Reuben says "don't leave until tuesday," but 47 hours, 58 minutes, and 30 seconds is exactly 48 hours minus ninety seconds. Counting from a Thursday start, that ends Saturday night, not Tuesday. It may be intentional, with Brick quietly imposing her own hard stop. It may also be an arithmetic slip. The chat doesn't say which.
